paragraphs.text: Li et al. (2016) used exome and candidate panel sequencing to study 2 unrelated children with epileptic encephalopathy. Both children had the same de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the GRIN2D gene, c.1999G-A (V667I). The mutation lies in the M3 transmembrane domain of GluN2D, a region involved in channel gating. Functional studies showed that the mutation caused a gain of function. It increased glutamate and glycine potency 2-fold and channel open probability 6-fold. It also reduced the receptor's sensitivity to endogenous negative modulators such as extracellular protons and prolonged the deactivation time course after glutamate removal. When cultured neurons were transfected with human GRIN2D cDNA carrying the mutation, they showed dendritic swelling and cell death, suggesting excitotoxicity from NMDA receptor overactivation.

paragraphs.text: Tsuchida et al. (2018) used whole-exome sequencing to study 3 unrelated patients with severe developmental delay and intractable epilepsy. Each patient had a different novel heterozygous missense variant in the GRIN2D gene. The altered residues were highly conserved across vertebrates and among the 4 GluN2 subunits. Based on structural analysis, the authors concluded that all 3 variants probably impair GluN2D function, either by affecting intersubunit interaction or by altering channel gating.

paragraphs.text: Li et al. (2016) tested FDA-approved NMDA receptor antagonists against the mutant receptors in vitro. Based on these results, both of their patients were given oral memantine, and seizure burden and development improved mildly to moderately. The older proband later developed refractory status epilepticus, which improved dramatically on electroclinical measures after treatment with ketamine and magnesium. The authors suggested that NMDA receptor antagonists may be useful as add-on epilepsy therapy in patients with GRIN2D gain-of-function mutations.

paragraphs.text: Li et al. (2016) found a recurrent de novo heterozygous c.1999G-A transition in the GRIN2D gene in 2 unrelated children with epileptic encephalopathy (DEE46). The mutation results in a val667-to-ile (V667I) substitution in the M3 transmembrane domain of GluN2D and was identified by exome and candidate panel sequencing. In functional studies, the mutation caused a gain of function. It increased glutamate and glycine potency 2-fold, increased channel open probability 6-fold, reduced sensitivity to extracellular protons, and prolonged deactivation. Cultured neurons transfected with the mutant cDNA showed dendritic swelling and cell death.
